hypothesis: The compound selectively targets an enzyme or enzymatic complex required exclusively during active cell division to synthesize or remodel a rigid, cross-linked structural polymer that exists in bacterial cell walls but has no counterpart in mammalian cell membranes or cytoskeleton. Inhibition of this cross-linking step prevents the wall from bearing turgor pressure, causing osmotic lysis without any direct effect on protein, nucleic acid, or energy metabolism.
mechanism: Actively dividing bacteria must continuously incorporate new structural polymer into their cell wall to accommodate growth; the compound irreversibly blocks the final transpeptidation cross-linking step that confers tensile strength to this polymer. As internal osmotic pressure (turgor) is not balanced by an intact, cross-linked wall, the membrane is forced outward, the cell deforms into a sphere or irregular shape, and eventually the membrane ruptures, releasing cytoplasmic contents. Mammalian cells lack this polymer entirely and rely on a lipid bilayer plus cytoskeletal proteins for structural integrity, so no equivalent vulnerability exists; stationary-phase bacteria survive because wall-remodeling enzymes are inactive and no new polymer insertion is attempted.
observations_explained: Bactericidal but not bacteriostatic outcome in dividing cells (lysis rather than mere growth arrest)
Reversibility of the block in stationary phase — polymer integrity is maintained when no new synthesis is attempted
Selective toxicity window between effective bacterial dose and mammalian no-effect dose (therapeutic index) explained by complete absence of target in host
Morphological progression from rod to sphere to ghost, consistent with loss of wall geometry before membrane failure
Gram-positive selectivity relative to gram-negative bacteria, explained by accessibility of the cross-linking enzyme through a thick, exposed peptidoglycan layer versus an outer membrane barrier
Efficacy unaffected by supplementing protein or nucleic acid synthesis inhibitors, confirming orthogonal mechanism
Hypertonic medium rescues bacteria from lysis without restoring wall integrity, consistent with osmotic rather than biochemical killing
parsimony_justification: Posits a single molecular target (the transpeptidase catalyzing cross-link formation in a bacterium-specific polymer) to explain all observations without invoking effects on metabolism, membrane lipids, or multiple pathways; requires no new entities beyond the known existence of bacterial cell-wall polymer and the turgor pressure differential.
novelty_justification: Rather than merely asserting 'cell-wall inhibition' as a retrieved fact, the abductive step constructs the explanatory logic from the observations upward: division-dependence implies the target is engaged only during active polymer remodeling; morphological swelling and lysis imply structural rather than metabolic failure; mammalian sparing implies the target polymer is phylogenetically absent from the host — together these constrain the Case specifically to cross-link formation in a division-coupled, bacteria-exclusive structural polymer, a mechanistic framing derived from the evidence rather than retrieved from memory.

candidate_survey.label: retrieval
candidate_survey.description: The compound inhibits cell-wall peptidoglycan synthesis, specifically the transpeptidase step, causing lysis in dividing bacteria; mammalian cells lack peptidoglycan.

candidate_survey.label: historical_decoy
candidate_survey.description: The compound acts as a detergent-like surfactant that disrupts bacterial membranes selectively due to differences in membrane lipid composition between bacteria and mammalian cells; division-dependence arises because membrane surface area expands during growth, increasing susceptibility.

candidate_survey.label: abductive
candidate_survey.description: The compound specifically inhibits the cross-linking enzyme that joins nascent polymer strands into a load-bearing network during active wall remodeling, a step uniquely required during division; the absence of this polymer class in mammalian cells and the mechanochemical (osmotic) rather than metabolic mode of killing together explain all observed selectivity, morphology, and reversibility data.
